title: The flight
hookLine: the palace asleep, the gates opening, the horse's hooves muffled (Buddhacarita 5)

cards: Before he leaves, he asks. That's the part of the flight that's easy to forget. The prince comes back from the field, goes to his father, bows, and says it out loud: let me go and become a wanderer.
The king weeps. Not yet, he says. You're young.

Wait. Then the prince makes an offer. Promise me four things, and I'll stay: that my life won't end in death, that sickness won't take my health, that age won't take my youth, that misfortune won't take what I have.
The king can't promise any of them. Nobody could. And so the asking ends, and the night begins.

teach.b: First, the sleeping palace. Back in his rooms the women play music for him as always, but the poem says the gods send a heavy sleep over them, and they fall where they are, instruments still in their arms.
Year one stood in that room; tonight the poem only passes through it on the way to the door. Second, the horse. The prince wakes Chandaka, his attendant, and asks for Kanthaka, his horse.
Chandaka brings him, and the prince speaks to the horse as to a friend, asking him to carry him well this one time.
Third, the gates. All his life this palace has been a machine for keeping the prince in and the world out: heavy doors, bars, guards.
Tonight, the poem says, gates that took strength to move swing open by themselves, without a sound. The city sleeps on. Fourth, the look back.

teach.h: A VOW TO THE FAR SHORE.
teach.b: Outside the city the prince turns toward it and vows not to come back until he has seen the far shore of birth and death. Then he rides on into the dark.
A father built walls: a cleared road, a garden, a friend's advice, a palace full of music. One by one, they gave. Tonight, the last one does.

how: The prince's leaving, often called the great going forth, is remembered in Buddhist art and at festivals, and in Theravada countries young men about to ordain sometimes ride in procession on a horse or are carried, recalling the prince's ride out of the city.

o: the prince's night departure from the palace
a journey on a flying horse to heaven
the prince's escape from enemies at war

games.q: the night of the flight: tap the pairs.

s: in the poem, the prince slips away without ever asking his father
he asks first, and offers to stay if the king can promise him four things.
the king promises the prince he will never grow old
he can't promise it. no one could.
in the poem, the gates open without a sound
the doors that kept the world out open on their own.

games.q: you're the prince. you've decided to leave, but your father loves you and rules the palace. what do you do first?
o: go to him and ask, out loud.
ask a friend to decide for him.
games.why: he asks his father. the king refuses, and the prince offers to stay if he can be promised he won't die, sicken, age or lose what he has.

practice: Stand if you can, or stay seated and move just your hands, and move as if everyone in the house were asleep: slow, soft, each foot set down without a sound, a cup lifted and lowered without a click.
Notice how much attention quiet takes, and how the room seems to grow when you stop making noise in it. Then sit, and rest in the hush you made.

wordCard.voice: The flight. The prince asks his father first, is refused, then leaves at night on Kanthaka with Chandaka, through gates that open on their own. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the gates open. He asked first, and then he went. See you tomorrow.
